input.reasoning:
Sizing approach: converted story points to engineering hours using a baseline of ~5 hours/point for full-stack effort (backend+frontend+QA+devops combined), calibrated per task based on its nature (pure backend, pure UI, infra, data migration, etc). Total backlog points = 5+8+8+13+8+5+13+21+8+8+5+5+8+13+8+5+8+13+8+8+5+8+5+8 = 200 points.

Role allocation logic:
- Backend Developer (1.5 FTE): owns API/business logic tasks - auth, RBAC, payments, migration, GDPR, audit log, email service, search, multi-currency, rate limiting, contract tests. Heaviest load given 1.5 FTE capacity.
- Frontend Developer (1.0 FTE): owns UI-heavy tasks - design system, dashboard, invoice UI, ticket UI, admin back-office, analytics, responsive layout, accessibility.
- QA Engineer (0.6 FTE): testing across all tasks, weighted more heavily on payment, RBAC, migration, GDPR, 2FA (high risk areas).
- DevOps Engineer (0.4 FTE): CI/CD, observability, decommissioning, migration infra support, rate limiting infra.

Capacity check (assuming a ~4 month / ~17 week delivery window, standard for a backlog this size):
- Backend: 1.5 FTE * 17 weeks * 40h = 1020h available
- Frontend: 1.0 FTE * 17 weeks * 40h = 680h available
- QA: 0.6 FTE * 17 weeks * 40h = 408h available
- DevOps: 0.4 FTE * 17 weeks * 40h = 272h available

Allocated hours below fit within these envelopes with some buffer for meetings/PM overhead already implicitly excluded (no PM role on rate card, so none allocated - flagged as assumption).

Per-task estimates were built bottom-up (hours per role per task), then summed per role. This gives:
Backend: ~940h, Frontend: ~610h, QA: ~370h, DevOps: ~230h — all within capacity, with Backend and Frontend running close to full utilization (indicating tight but feasible staffing), consistent with the note that Backend Developer capacity is the primary constraint given the volume of API-heavy work (payments, RBAC, migration, GDPR, 2FA, multi-currency).

Non-labour costs: Stripe integration test/sandbox fees, cloud infra for staging/CI, data migration tooling/Oracle export licensing, contingency for third-party audit (accessibility, security review of auth/payments).

Priority breakdown computed by summing estimated task costs (labour only, allocated pro-rata) grouped by priority tag.

Reductions identified: descoping Low-priority items (support ticket sync, admin back-office, usage analytics, contract tests, legacy decommission) which total 39 points/~19.5% of backlog; deferring multi-currency to phase 2; trimming QA on low-risk UI tasks.

Scenarios: P50 = base estimate, P80 = +18% for integration/migration risk, P95 = +35% for major risk realization (migration data quality issues, Stripe reconciliation edge cases, timeline slip on thinly-staffed DevOps role).

scenarios.name: P80 - Likely with integration/migration risk buffer
P95 - High risk realized (migration, Stripe, staffing constraints)

assumptions: No historical actuals (real spend data) are available for this project yet; estimate is based purely on backlog sizing and rate card, not past performance.
Assumed a delivery window of ~17 weeks (4 months), giving Backend 1020h, Frontend 680h, QA 408h and DevOps 272h theoretical capacity; allocated hours were kept below these ceilings.

Backend Developer (1.5 FTE) is the most heavily loaded role given the volume of API-heavy work (auth, RBAC, payments, migration, GDPR, 2FA, multi-currency); at ~940 of 1020 available hours it is staffed close to its ceiling and is a scheduling risk if any backend task slips.

DevOps Engineer (0.4 FTE) is thinly staffed relative to infra-touching tasks (CI/CD, migration infra, observability, rate limiting, decommissioning); flagged as a risk of delay rather than a cost risk.
No Project Manager / Scrum Master / BA role exists on the rate card, so no coordination overhead is costed; assumed the roles self-organize or a client-side PM exists.

Story points were converted using an approximate 5 hours/point blended rate across all roles combined, adjusted per task type (e.g., migration and payments weighted higher due to complexity and reconciliation/testing needs).
QA effort was weighted more heavily toward Urgent/High priority and compliance-sensitive tasks (payments, RBAC, GDPR, 2FA, migration) and lighter on cosmetic/UI-only tasks.
Multi-currency (PW-14) assumed to use a third-party FX rate feed; no separate vendor licensing cost included beyond contingency.
Legacy data migration (PW-8) assumed one-time cutover with a fallback/reconciliation pass, not a phased multi-year migration.
Non-labour contingency of 5% of labour cost added to cover minor unforeseen tooling/license costs.

reductions.description: Descope all Low-priority items this phase (PW-12 ticket sync, PW-18 admin back-office, PW-19 usage analytics, PW-23 contract tests, PW-24 legacy decommission) to a later phase
reductions.effect: Removes ~39 backlog points of Low-priority work from labour lines entirely, deferring to a phase 2 backlog

reductions.description: Defer Multi-currency support (PW-14) to phase 2; ship single-currency (USD) first
reductions.effect: Removes 13 points of backend/frontend/QA effort tied to FX handling and settlement logic

reductions.description: Reduce QA allocation on low-risk cosmetic tasks (design system, mobile responsive layout, accessibility pass) by ~30%, relying more on automated visual regression tests
reductions.effect: Cuts roughly 50 QA hours from UI-only tasks while keeping full QA depth on payments/auth/migration

reductions.description: Use a managed migration service or Stripe-supplied reconciliation tooling instead of custom-built tooling for PW-8/PW-7
reductions.effect: Reduces backend build hours on migration tooling and payment reconciliation by leveraging vendor tooling; partially offset by tooling license cost already in non-labour

reductions.description: Push non-critical non-labour spend (accessibility audit, security review) to post-launch hardening sprint
reductions.effect: Removes third-party accessibility audit and security review from initial budget, performed in a later hardening cycle instead
